acceptedAnswer.text: For most patients, composite bonding is a comfortable procedure that does not require anaesthetic, as little or no drilling is involved. You may feel mild pressure during the application process, but significant discomfort is not typical. If the notch is close to the nerve or involves sensitivity, your dentist may discuss whether local anaesthetic is appropriate. Any concerns about comfort should be discussed openly with your dental team before treatment begins.

mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups, composite bonding typically lasts between five and seven years, though this varies depending on the patient's bite, habits, and how well they care for their teeth. Bonded areas may occasionally need polishing or small repairs during this time. Your dentist will monitor the bonding at routine appointments and advise you when maintenance or replacement may be needed.

mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding fix a gap as well as a notch between teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding can sometimes address both a notch and a small gap between teeth in the same treatment, as the resin can be shaped to build up the tooth edge and close minor spaces. However, larger gaps or more complex spacing concerns may be better addressed through orthodontic treatment or alternative cosmetic approaches. A dentist will assess your specific situation and discuss which options are most appropriate for your case.

mainEntity.name: Will the composite bonding look natural?

acceptedAnswer.text: Modern composite resin materials are designed to closely match the colour, translucency, and sheen of natural tooth enamel. Your dentist will carefully shade-match the resin before treatment. The results can look very natural in most cases, though exact outcomes depend on factors such as the location of the tooth, surrounding tooth colour, and the extent of the area being treated. Your dentist will discuss realistic expectations with you during the consultation.

Because composite bonding in most cases requires minimal preparation of the tooth surface, it is generally considered a more reversible option than treatments such as porcelain veneers or crowns, which involve more significant tooth reduction. However, "reversible" does not mean entirely without impact — any treatment involves some change to the tooth's surface. This is another reason why thorough pre-treatment discussion with your dentist is important.

mainEntity.name: What if my notch is caused by grinding?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your dentist identifies bruxism (teeth grinding or clenching) as a contributing cause of the notch, they may recommend addressing this before proceeding with composite bonding. A custom-made occlusal splint or night guard can help protect your teeth and any bonded surfaces from further wear. Proceeding with cosmetic treatment without managing an underlying grinding habit may reduce the longevity of the results.
